body:
When does blockchain offer a useful advantage?

Blockchain is most useful when several organisations need to contribute to a common record, want to verify one another's entries and require a history that is difficult to alter secretly. It can reduce disagreements caused by separate, inconsistent databases.

The choice depends on the problem. If one department controls a register and every other user accepts that department as the authoritative record keeper, a conventional database may provide the necessary service more simply.

Verification of educational and government certificates

Institutions issue certificates to establish qualifications, identity-related facts or eligibility. A blockchain-based verification system can maintain information about the issue and status of a certificate. A verifier can compare the certificate presented by a person with the issuing institution's recognised record.

For example, an educational board may publish an authorised record that a particular certificate was issued. A recruiting organisation can verify that the certificate corresponds to the issuing board's record. If the certificate is later revoked or corrected, the verification process should consider the latest authorised status.

The record helps detect fabricated or altered documents. It does not guarantee that an institution followed the correct procedure before issuing an authentic certificate.

Supply chains and the movement of goods

A supply chain connects producers, transporters, warehouses, wholesalers and retailers. These parties may need to know when goods were produced, dispatched, received or transferred.

A shared ledger can record those events and provide an auditable history across participating organisations. In a medicine supply chain, such a history may help trace the recorded movement of a batch through distribution.

Traceability means that recorded movements can be followed. It does not, by itself, establish that a medicine has the correct chemical composition, that a package was never replaced or that every physical inspection was performed correctly. Those conclusions require additional controls.

Land records and ownership information

Land administration involves changes resulting from sale, inheritance, partition and other legally recognised events. A shared register may help maintain an auditable record of submitted changes and their authorisation.

However, recording a claim is different from legally establishing ownership. Government procedures, documentary evidence and the applicable laws determine the legal consequences of a land transaction. A blockchain entry alone cannot settle every title dispute.

Financial records and digital assets

Blockchain systems can record transfers of digital assets and support shared transaction histories between participating institutions. They may also be used for selected financial verification, reconciliation and monitoring functions.

The concepts must be kept separate:

  • Blockchain: Technology for maintaining a shared, tamper-resistant ledger.
  • Cryptocurrency: A category of digital assets that can use blockchain networks.
  • Digital payment: Electronic transfer of value, which does not necessarily use blockchain.
  • Central bank digital currency: Digital central-bank money; its existence does not by itself establish that it operates on a public blockchain.

Other public-service applications

Distributed ledger systems may be considered for government document verification, judicial record tracking, cross-department information exchange and verification of communication-related records. The need for privacy, authorised access and dependable correction procedures is especially important in these applications.

India's National Informatics Centre (NIC) identifies blockchain products for certificate verification, document verification, drug logistics, judiciary-related records and property-related records. Their presence demonstrates particular implementations; it does not mean that every certificate, land transaction or judicial record in India is maintained on blockchain.

Prelims focus

  • Certificate systems can use blockchain to support authenticity and status verification.
  • Supply-chain systems can record the movement of goods across organisations.
  • Blockchain traceability does not independently prove the physical quality of goods.
  • A land-record entry is not a substitute for legal determination of title.
  • Digital payments and cryptocurrencies are not synonyms for blockchain.
  • Trap: A service being online or digitally signed does not prove that it uses blockchain.

[NIST, Blockchain, potential applications in supply chains, data registries, digital identification and records management, consulted 5 November 2026; UK National Cyber Security Centre, Distributed Ledger Technology, Determining the Suitability of Distributed Ledger Technology and Example Applications sections, consulted 5 November 2026; National Informatics Centre, Centre of Excellence in Blockchain Technology, Products and Live Chains, consulted 5 November 2026.]

title: Practical Uses of Blockchain in Public Services and Business

body:
Who is allowed to participate?

Not all blockchain networks allow the same people to read records, submit transactions or validate blocks. These permissions depend on the network's design and governance.

A permissionless network generally allows participants to join and perform permitted activities without prior approval from a central membership authority. A permissioned network restricts selected activities, especially validation or record submission, to authorised participants.

FeaturePermissionless networkPermissioned network
ParticipationGenerally open under network rulesSelected activities require authorisation
ValidatorsEligible participants follow open protocol rulesApproved participants validate records
Typical useOpen blockchain systemsNetworks of identified organisations
Access controlDetermined by open protocol rulesDefined by responsible network administrators or members

Public or private visibility is a related but different question. A network may restrict who validates records while allowing broader public verification of selected information. Thus, permissioned does not automatically mean that no information can be viewed publicly.

What is blockchain governance?

Blockchain governance is the set of rules and decision-making arrangements used to operate, supervise and change a blockchain network.

Consensus determines how the network agrees on records. Governance determines who sets those rules, who may participate and how the system deals with change or disputes. A network can be technically distributed while still having clearly identified organisations responsible for its administration.

Important governance decisions

  • Membership: Which departments or organisations may join, and who may remove access?
  • Authority: Who can issue records, validate entries, view restricted information and revoke permissions?
  • Data protection: Which information can be shared, and which sensitive data must remain protected or outside the ledger?
  • Correction: How are inaccurate records corrected, cancelled or marked as superseded?
  • Disputes: Who investigates conflicting claims and who makes the legally or administratively binding decision?
  • Upgrades: Who approves changes to software, smart contracts and operating rules?

Benefits and limits should be assessed together

Useful properties of a well-designed distributed ledger may include a common record history, stronger evidence of unauthorised alterations, reduced need for repeated reconciliation and greater auditability.

These benefits come with possible difficulties:

  • Privacy: Copies of data held by several participants can create additional confidentiality risks unless access is carefully controlled.
  • Performance: Coordinating agreement across a network may add delay and processing costs compared with a simple database.
  • Energy: Some consensus methods, particularly large Proof-of-Work networks, can be energy-intensive; this does not apply equally to every blockchain.
  • Incorrect inputs: A tamper-resistant record can still preserve a false statement.
  • Security: Poor software, stolen signing keys or compromised administrators can undermine the system.
  • Legal authority: A digital record does not remove the need for authorised decisions and applicable procedures.

Choosing the appropriate technology

Suppose 4 government departments need a common register and each department is allowed to submit particular kinds of records. A permissioned blockchain may be considered if no single department should be able to change the common history alone and the shared audit trail provides a clear benefit.

By contrast, if a single department issues all records, maintains the authoritative database and merely allows citizens to check their status, a conventional secure database may be sufficient. Blockchain should be selected for a defined need, not merely because it is a newer technology.

Governance versus consensus: Governance establishes participation, responsibility and operating rules. Consensus applies the established network rules to agree on records. Neither replaces legal or administrative accountability.

Prelims focus

  • Permissionless networks generally allow open participation under protocol rules.
  • Permissioned networks restrict selected activities to authorised participants.
  • Permissioned networks are not necessarily invisible to the public.
  • Governance covers membership, permissions, corrections, disputes and upgrades.
  • Blockchain may add cost, delay and privacy concerns.
  • Trap: Technical decentralisation does not mean that a network has no governance.

[UK National Cyber Security Centre, Distributed Ledger Technology, Distributed Ledger Technology, Determining the Suitability of Distributed Ledger Technology and Alternative Technologies sections, consulted 5 November 2026; NIST, Blockchain, overview of validation, consensus and tamper resistance, consulted 5 November 2026; Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, Press Information Bureau release on Vishvasya-Blockchain Technology Stack, 4 September 2024.]

pictures.alt: Connected governance decisions control membership, record approval, later corrections and dispute resolution, plus sensitive information access and upgrades.
pictures.caption: Blockchain governance connects membership, record approval, correction and accountability.

title: Permissioned Blockchains, Network Governance and Practical Limitations

body:
National Strategy on Blockchain

The Government of India's Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) released the National Strategy on Blockchain on 3 December 2021.

The strategy aimed to encourage research, innovation and application development and to support trusted digital services through shared blockchain infrastructure. A strategy sets policy direction; it is not the same as a claim that every proposed application has already been implemented.

National Blockchain Framework and Vishvasya

On 4 September 2024, MeitY launched the Vishvasya-Blockchain Technology Stack as part of the National Blockchain Framework (NBF). The stack was designed to provide Blockchain-as-a-Service (BaaS) for developing and operating permissioned blockchain applications.

Blockchain-as-a-Service means that participating organisations can use a shared technical platform for applications rather than each organisation building all the underlying infrastructure independently.

The government's launch announcement identified geographically distributed infrastructure at National Informatics Centre data centres in Bhubaneswar, Pune and Hyderabad.

Important named components

InitiativeMain purposeVerified milestone
National Strategy on BlockchainPolicy direction for trusted blockchain-based digital servicesReleased 3 December 2021
Vishvasya-Blockchain Technology StackShared permissioned blockchain infrastructure and servicesLaunched 4 September 2024
NBFLiteLightweight sandbox for startups and academic institutionsUnveiled 4 September 2024
PraamaanikBlockchain-enabled verification of mobile application originUnveiled 4 September 2024
National Blockchain PortalPortal associated with national blockchain initiativesUnveiled 4 September 2024

A sandbox is a controlled environment in which a system can be tested and developed. The existence of NBFLite does not establish that every experimental application has been deployed for public use.

National Informatics Centre blockchain services

The National Informatics Centre (NIC) operates a Centre of Excellence in Blockchain Technology. Its official product and live-chain listings identify several applications:

  • Certificate Chain: Supports verification of authorised certificates.
  • Document Chain: Supports verification of government and other recognised documents.
  • Drug Logistics Chain: Supports records related to the movement of medicines.
  • Judiciary Chain: Addresses blockchain-based records in judiciary-related workflows.
  • Property Chain: Addresses property-related records.
  • ICJS Chain: Appears among the listed live chains associated with the Inter-operable Criminal Justice System.

These are examples of specific systems and services. Their listing does not establish nationwide blockchain coverage of all records in each sector.

Live applications are different from proofs of concept

A proof of concept (PoC) is a limited exercise intended to demonstrate whether an idea or technical approach can work. It should not be confused with a fully deployed, statewide or nationwide public service.

NIC separately lists proofs of concept concerning Assam land records, blood banks, GST Chain and the Public Distribution System. Their classification as PoCs is important: the listing does not, by itself, establish that these applications have become nationwide operational services.

Dates and implementation status

At the 5 November 2026 content cutoff, the historical milestones of 3 December 2021 and 4 September 2024 are established launch dates. The named NIC products and PoCs are those identified on the official Centre of Excellence website consulted for this lesson. Their status should not be extended to every government department or geographic area without separate deployment evidence.

Prelims focus

  • MeitY released the National Strategy on Blockchain on 3 December 2021.
  • Vishvasya-Blockchain Technology Stack was launched on 4 September 2024.
  • Vishvasya supports permissioned Blockchain-as-a-Service.
  • NBFLite is intended for startups and academia.
  • Praamaanik concerns verification of mobile application origin.
  • Trap: A proof of concept is not evidence of nationwide deployment.

[Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, Press Information Bureau, Rajeev Chandrasekhar Launches National Strategy on Blockchain, 3 December 2021; Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, Press Information Bureau, Government Launches Vishvasya-Blockchain Technology Stack, 4 September 2024; National Informatics Centre, Centre of Excellence in Blockchain Technology, Products, Live Chains and POC sections, consulted 5 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: A blockchain framework provides shared infrastructure for applications that organisations develop and operate.
